transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, it's just... I don't even know where to start, but I came in because I just feel like I got this motor running inside me all day long. Like an actual engine just humming and vibrating right in my chest and my legs, from the second I open my eyes in the morning. It's driving me up the wall, it really is. 

Like, if I have to sit still anywhere—say we go to church, right? Sitting in those hard wooden pews while the preacher is going on and on... I feel completely trapped. Like I'm locked in a tiny cage and the walls are closing in. My legs start bouncing, my skin starts crawling, and I just have to get up or do something, anything, just to get that energy out before I explode. 

And it ain't just church. It was the exact same thing out there in your clinic waiting room just a minute ago. They told me to take a seat, but I just couldn't do it for more than two minutes, I was pacing a hole in the carpet looking at all the posters on the wall. Even at home! I'm not working right now, so I'm around the house a lot, and you'd think a guy could just sit on the couch and relax, watch a little TV, but nope. The second I sit down, that motor kicks into high gear and I feel that trapped feeling all over again, and I'm right back up on my feet walking around, messing with stuff, just moving. It just never shuts off, doc.
Do you have trouble focusing on tasks or activities?

Focus? Well, yeah, I guess you could say that. It's... it's mostly when people are talking to me, you know? Like, say folks are trying to talk through something important with me. Could be my buddy figuring out ride times 'cause my truck's busted, or my sister going over pantry lists 'cause she wants me to help out around the house since I ain't working, or even just the church plans for the weekend... 

I really do try to pay attention, I swear I do. I stand there, and I listen real good at first. I'm nodding, I'm looking right at 'em, but then... I don't know, it's like my brain just unhooks itself. My mind just slips off. I'll start thinking about that motor running in my chest, or I'll see a crack in the drywall, or I'm just... gone. Just completely drifting off somewhere else. And their mouth is still moving, and they're still talking, but it's just noise to me at that point. 

And then they stop and look at me, waiting for me to answer, and I realize I completely missed the pieces I really needed to hear. The times, the grocery items, all of it. And then they get all hot under the collar, thinking I don't care about what they're saying or that I'm being disrespectful, but I ain't! I'm really not. It just... it just slips away from me, doc. No matter how hard I try to hold onto the words, they just wash right over me and I'm left standing there looking like a fool, having to ask 'em to repeat the whole thing all over again.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting with your hands or feet when you're sitting still?

Oh, man, constantly. It’s exactly like I was saying about that motor, right? If I actually manage to force my backside into a chair, my hands and feet just... they just take over. 

Like, I’ll be sitting there, and I really am trying to be respectful—especially if my sister is sitting me down to talk about chores, or if we're eating dinner or something. I know I’m supposed to just sit quiet and act right, but my leg... it just starts going a mile a minute. Bouncing up and down like I’m pumping a gas pedal over and over. And if it ain’t my leg doing the bouncing, it’s my hands. I’ll be tapping my fingers on the arm of the chair, just tap-tap-tapping away, not even realizing I’m doing it until somebody glares at me. 

Or I'll grab whatever is sitting near me—a napkin, a bottle cap, a piece of string, don't matter what it is—and I’m just twisting it up, rolling it around and pulling on it in my hands the whole entire time. My sister actually slaps my hand sometimes, tells me to stop fidgeting like a little kid. And I feel bad, you know, 'cause like I said, even when I'm trying to be respectful and give 'em my full attention, my body just won't listen. It’s like all that nervous energy just leaks right out of my fingers and toes, and no matter how hard I stare at my own hands and tell 'em to stop, they just keep on moving.
Did you have trouble sitting still or paying attention when you were a kid?

Well, yeah... yeah, it goes way back. I mean, way back to when I was just a little bitty guy in school. I never could sit still, not even then. I remember my teachers—Mrs. Gable in third grade, Mr. Henderson in fifth—they were always moving my seat. Always. I’d be in the front row one week, then back in the corner by the encyclopedias the next week, then right next to the teacher's desk. And they'd do that because I just could not stay put in my chair, doc. I mean, it was impossible. My body just had to move, same as now. 

And it wasn't just the moving around, either. I was always talking out of turn. Like, the teacher would ask a question, and instead of raising my hand and waiting like you're supposed to, I'd just blurt out the answer, or whatever popped into my head, really. I just couldn't hold it in. The words would just fly right out of my mouth before I even realized I was opening it. They used to get so mad at me, telling me I was disrupting the whole class. 

And man, getting through a whole class period? Forget about it. I'd be watching that big round clock on the wall, listening to it tick, and I swear, ten minutes before the bell was even supposed to ring, I was already out of my seat. I'd be jumping up, trying to pack my bag, ready to bolt out the door, and I got in so much trouble for that. Sent to the principal's office, notes sent home to my mama... it was just a constant struggle, day in and day out, trying to force myself to just sit there and act like all the other kids who didn't seem to have that same motor running inside them.
Do you often interrupt others when they're speaking?

Interrupting? Oh, man... yeah. Yeah, I do that all the time, and I really, really don't mean to. It’s just like I was saying about school, how I’d blurt things out? It’s exactly like that, but worse now because adults get a lot more offended than teachers do when you cut 'em off. 

It’s like... I’ll be talking to somebody, right? Could be anybody. Like the pastor down at the church, or my cousin when he comes over to bum a smoke, or even the lady who runs the community food pantry where my sister makes me go get the boxes. They’ll be right in the middle of a sentence, trying to ask me a question or tell me how something works, and I swear, my brain just jumps the gun. I hear the first half of what they're saying, and my mind just races ahead, and before I can even bite my tongue, the answer is already flying out of my mouth. 

I just... I jump right in. I don't even wait for them to finish breathing, let alone finish their sentence. And the worst part—the absolute worst part, doc—is that half the time, because I didn't let them finish, I end up answering the completely wrong thing! Like, the pantry lady will be saying, "Do you want the canned peaches or the..." and I'm already yelling "Peaches!" before she can even say "pears," but maybe she was gonna say "or the extra box of cereal," and now I've missed out, you know? 

And it makes people so mad. My cousin gets real loud about it, tells me to shut my trap and let a man speak. The pastor just gets this... this look on his face, like he’s real disappointed in me, like I’m just a rude, ill-mannered guy who don't respect his elders. And I try to explain, I try to say, "Look, I'm sorry, it just slipped out," but they don't get it. They think I'm doing it on purpose, like I think what I have to say is more important than what they're saying. But it ain't that at all! It's just that motor again, doc. It pushes the words up my throat and out my mouth before my brain can tell my lips to stay shut. And then I'm just standing there, feeling like a jerk, apologizing again and again, and they're just glaring at me. It happens every single day, I swear it does.
Have you ever lost a job or had problems in your relationships because of your difficulty sitting still, focusing, or interrupting others?

Jobs? Well, I ain't actually been working in a good long while, so I can't even really speak on that right now, but relationships? Oh, man. My whole life is just... it's just a string of people getting fed up with me. It’s exactly what you’re saying. It ruins everything. 

It’s like... people just flat out stopped trusting me. And not with big, complicated stuff, doc, but with the simplest things in the world. Take the folks down at the church, for instance. The pastor used to ask me to help out by giving some of the older folks rides to Sunday service or Wednesday night supper, you know, since I got my old truck and I’m around. But I’d get so antsy waiting in their driveways, tapping on the steering wheel, that I'd end up driving off to go do something else for "just a minute" and completely forget to go back and get 'em. Or I'd be talking over them the whole ride, making them nervous. So now? They don't even ask me for rides anymore. They just find somebody else and leave me out of it. 

And it’s the exact same thing down at the pantry. I told you about the lady who runs it, right? Well, she used to let me volunteer, helping her sort out the donations and the supplies. But I’d be moving way too fast, bouncing around, putting the canned green beans where the baby formula goes, or I’d interrupt her right when she was trying to read off the inventory list, messing up her whole count. Now she won't trust me with the supplies at all. She just hands me my box at the door and practically shooes me away. 

But the worst is my family. My sister, she’s the one who lets me stay with her, and I try to earn my keep, I really do. But she won't even trust me to handle a basic appointment anymore. Like, she’ll say, "Stay right here in the living room, the cable guy is coming between twelve and two." But I can't just sit there for two hours! I'll go out back to tinker with the lawnmower, or I'll get to pacing and wander off down the street, and I completely miss the guy knocking. 

She gets so mad, doc. She just looks at me and says she can't rely on me for absolutely nothing. And it just... it breaks my heart, you know? It really does. Because people at the church, the pantry, my own family... they all just look at me like I'm a liability now. Like I'm just a burden. I feel like I keep letting everybody down, over and over again, even when I genuinely, with all my heart, just mean to help. I want to be helpful! But my body and my mouth just run off without me, and I end up ruining it every single time.
Have you experienced these symptoms of restlessness and difficulty focusing consistently throughout your life, or have they changed over time?

Well, see, like I was telling you before, I’ve always been a restless kind of guy. I always had that motor running since I was just a kid in school. But... but it ain't always been *this* bad, doc. I mean, I used to just kind of scrape by, you know? I'd get in trouble, sure, but I survived it. But as far as it being this hard to manage—where I’m just completely messing up every little thing and letting everybody down left and right? That really shifted on me about two years and two months ago. 

I know exactly how long it’s been, too, because that’s right exactly when my older relative... well, her health took a real bad turn. She got real sick, started having trouble just getting up out of her chair, and she couldn't really do for herself no more. And since I’m the one not working, you know, it all just kind of fell on me. The family looked at me and said I had to step up. 

So suddenly, I had to take on all these new responsibilities. I’m talking about having to remember a whole complicated schedule for her pills—which is like five different bottles, doc, all at different times of the day, some with food, some without—and I had to do all the grocery runs, and try to keep the house from falling apart, and make sure the bills actually get put in the mail instead of lost in my pockets. And I wanted to do it right, I really, genuinely did. 

But having all that extra weight on my shoulders... it just made everything short-circuit. It's like, the more I had to sit down and focus on, the worse the bouncing around and the blurting out got. Two years and two months of just drowning in it. Ever since her health changed and they piled all those responsibilities on my plate, it’s just been a total disaster. I try to sit down and sort her medications, and next thing I know I'm out in the yard pacing around, or I'm at the store and I interrupt the pharmacist when he's trying to explain her new prescription, and I end up bringing home the wrong instructions. It's just... it's been exactly two years and two months of feeling like I'm losing my mind because I just can't hold it all together, no matter how hard I try.
Have your symptoms of restlessness and difficulty focusing been present in multiple settings, such as at home, in social situations, and in other daily activities?

Well, yeah, doc, it's everywhere. I mean, like I was just telling you, it ain't just at the house with my sister, though Lord knows it's bad enough there. It's everywhere I go. It follows me around like... like my own shadow, you know? I used to think, maybe if I just get out of the house, maybe if I just go down to the hardware store to look at some tools or walk around the block, maybe I'd leave that jumpy, restless feeling behind on the porch. But it don't work like that. Not at all. 

I walk through the doors of a store, and boom, I'm tapping my feet in the aisle, picking things up, putting 'em down in the wrong spot, blurting things out to the cashiers before they even finish ringing me up. And then I go over to the church, and I'm doing the exact same thing to the pastor. And then I'm at the pantry, doing it there too. It don't matter if it's a Tuesday morning in my sister's living room or a Sunday night at the church supper. That motor inside me, it just keeps humming and humming, and it don't care where I'm standing or who I'm talking to. 

I really wish I could just turn it off, I really do. Because then maybe I could just have one place, you know? Just one single place where I could go and sit quiet and people wouldn't be getting all mad and disappointed at me. But I ain't got a place like that. Because no matter where I go, I gotta take my brain and my body with me, and they're the things causing all the trouble in the first place. So yeah, it's everywhere. Every single place I go, every single day, without fail. It just never stops.
Have you felt like your symptoms have significantly impacted your ability to function in daily life or maintain relationships?

Well, yeah, doc, I mean... that's exactly what I was pouring my heart out about right at the start, you know? It's just completely wrecked my day-to-day life. I mean, it's like I said before... the folks down at the church, the lady at the pantry, even my own family... they've all just flat out stopped trusting me with anything. 

And it's the simple things! They won't let me do the rides for the older folks no more, my sister won't trust me to handle a basic appointment at the house, they won't even let me near the supplies at the pantry to sort the cans. They just cut me right out of it all. And it ain't like I'm trying to be a bad person, or like I don't care. That's the part that really, truly gets me, doc, the part that just eats at me. I care so much. I really, genuinely mean to help them out. I want to be useful, you know? I want to earn my keep and be a good neighbor. 

But it's like... no matter how hard I try to just be a normal, helpful guy, my body just won't let me sit still long enough to do it right. I get antsy, I start pacing, my mouth runs off, and then I see that look on their faces. You know that look? That look of just pure, heavy disappointment. Like I'm just a big burden they gotta work around. It just breaks my heart, because I feel like I keep letting everybody down, every single day, even when I'm trying with all my heart to do the right thing. So yeah, it's impacted everything. It feels like it's ruined just about every relationship I got, to be honest with you.
Have you ever been unable to maintain a job or complete tasks at work due to your symptoms?

Well, doc, as far as a regular, punch-the-clock kind of paying job goes, I ain't been in the workforce for a good while now, mostly because of my lack of schooling and then having to be the one at home for my older relative. But if you're talking about completing tasks—like the work I try to do around the house or the volunteer work I was doing down at the pantry before they cut me out—oh man, it's... it's just a complete mess. 

I can tell you exactly how it goes, every single time. It don't matter how simple it is. I’ll start an errand for my relative, or I'll take on a job down at the pantry, and I always start out with the best of intentions. Like, the lady at the pantry will say, "Hey, go in the back and bring out all the boxes of canned beans and stack 'em on the second shelf." Or my sister will ask me to run to the pharmacy for her pills and grab some milk on the way back. And I hear 'em! I look 'em right in the eye, I nod my head, and I say, "I'm on it." 

And I do start it. I'll go right to the back room and grab that first box, or I'll drive straight to the pharmacy. But then... I end up doing just that very first part, and then my brain just completely drops the ball and I forget the rest of it. It's like the rest of the instructions just evaporate out of my head. I'll set that first box of beans down, get distracted by a spot on the floor or start pacing around because my legs get twitchy, and next thing I know I'm out in the parking lot talking to somebody or trying to fix a loose hinge on the door. 

And the worst part—the part that just makes me feel about two inches tall—is that I don't even realize I messed up until way after the fact. People always find out later that I never finished it. The pantry lady will come out an hour later and see one single box sitting in the middle of the aisle, or I'll get home and my sister will ask where her milk is, and I'm just standing there empty-handed feeling like a total fool. I start strong, doc, I really do, but I just can't seem to follow a job all the way through to the end to save my life.
Are there any particular situations or places where your symptoms seem to get worse?

Well, doc, I've been sitting here trying to think on that, trying to see if there's like... a specific trigger, you know? Like if the pantry is somehow worse than the church, or if being cooped up at my sister's house is worse than wandering around the hardware store. But honestly? No. I really can't say one place is worse than the other. It's not like... I don't know, it's not like an allergy where you walk into a room with a dog and suddenly you're sneezing worse than you were outside, you know what I mean? 

With me, it's just... it's always turned all the way up to the maximum. From the very minute my eyes pop open in the morning, that motor I was telling you about is just running hot. I could be sitting in a pitch-black, quiet room all by myself, or I could be standing in the middle of a crowded grocery store on a busy Saturday afternoon, and the feeling inside my skin is exactly the same. My legs still want to bounce right off the floor, my mouth still wants to run ahead of my brain, and I still forget what I'm doing halfway through doing it. 

I remember one time, my sister, she said to me, "Maybe you just don't do well in crowds. Maybe all those people at the church supper just get you too riled up." So I thought, okay, maybe she's onto something. I tried going down to the pond at the park early one Tuesday when absolutely nobody was there. Just me and a couple of ducks. And you'd think, okay, nice and peaceful, right? Maybe the jumpiness will settle down. But nope. Not even a little bit. I was pacing up and down the muddy bank, throwing the bread way too fast, talking out loud to myself, getting all wound up and distracted by a piece of trash floating in the water. 

So it ain't the crowds. And it ain't the quiet, either. It's just... me. It's just how my body is all the time, no matter what the scenery looks like or who's standing next to me. So I can't really point you to one specific situation where it spikes or gets worse, because it just feels plain awful and out of control everywhere I go.
Did you experience these symptoms before the age of 12?

Oh, absolutely, doc. I mean, way, way back before I was twelve. If you ask anybody who knew me when I was just a little guy, they would tell you the exact same thing. Back when I was a boy in school, it was just... well, it was a nightmare for everyone involved, to be honest. I remember my teachers, they were always, and I mean constantly, moving my seat around the room. They would put me in the front row, then move me to the back, then put my desk right up against theirs, thinking if they just found the magic spot, I would finally settle down. 

But it never worked, because I just could not stay put. My legs would be swinging, I would be leaning all over the place, dropping my pencils just so I had an excuse to crawl around on the floor and get out of that chair. And the talking, oh man. I talked out of turn all day long. A thought would pop into my head about a bug I saw outside or something, and I would just blurt it right out in the middle of a reading lesson. I never meant to be a bad kid or disrespectful to the teacher, but the words would just fall out of my mouth before my brain could even try to stop them. 

And waiting for the day to end? That was the absolute hardest part of the whole day. I was always getting in trouble for jumping up before class was done. The clock would be ticking down those last five minutes, and I would already be standing up, grabbing my bag, pacing by my desk while everyone else was still sitting quietly like they were supposed to. I just had this overwhelming feeling like my skin was too tight and I had to move right that very second, and I just could not wait for the bell. So yeah, it is definitely not a new problem. It has been getting me in hot water and making me feel like a nuisance since I was just a little kid trying to make it through the day.
Do you remember experiencing these symptoms before you were 7 years old?

Well, doc, now you are really testing my memory. Seven years old... man, that is going way, way back. I mean, I know for a fact I was a total handful before I was twelve, like I just told you with all that business about the teachers moving my desk around, but trying to pinpoint exactly what was happening when I was six or seven? That is just a complete blur to me. I remember little snippets of being that little, you know? Like I remember the color of the front porch on the house we rented back then—it was this really ugly peeling green color, and the wood was always giving me splinters—and I remember my sister pushing me into a sticker bush one time when we were playing in the yard. But as for how my body felt inside, or if I was getting in trouble for talking out of turn in the first grade... I just cannot rightly say for sure. 

My brain just does not hold onto specific ages and dates like that. It is like trying to catch smoke with your bare hands, it just slips right through your fingers. I know I was always a wild child. My mom used to tell everybody that I came out kicking and screaming and just never stopped moving from day one, but as far as actual solid memories of being exactly six years old and jumping out of my seat or pacing around? I cannot swear to it. It all just blends together into one big, long memory of always being in motion and always being in trouble. So if you need a hard yes or no about the age of seven, I am just gonna have to say I honestly do not know. I wish I could give you a better timeline, I really do, because I want to get to the bottom of this, but those early, early years are just plain gone from my head.
Did your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty focusing or following through on instructions, cause significant problems for you before the age of 7?

Well, doc, that's kind of the same boat as the last question, you know? It's just... it's really hard to say. I mean, you're asking about focusing and following instructions before I was seven, and like I was just saying, that whole time period is just a giant blur. I can't even remember what my first-grade teacher looked like, let alone if she was getting onto me for not paying attention or for not finishing a coloring sheet or whatever it is kids do at that age. 

I mean, I'm sure I was a handful. Like I said, my mom always said I was a wild child from day one. But was it because I couldn't focus? Or was it because I just couldn't sit still? Or maybe both? I just don't know. I remember my sister always telling me I never listened to her, but that could just be normal brother-sister stuff, right? She'd say, "I told you to put the blocks away," and I'd be off chasing a dog down the street. But did that start when I was five? Six? Eight? I honestly couldn't tell you. 

It's frustrating, I know. You're looking for these specific milestones, and I'm just sitting here giving you a whole lot of nothing. I wish I had a better memory for this stuff. I wish I could say, "Oh yeah, I remember my fifth birthday party, I couldn't even focus on blowing out the candles because I was too busy looking at a balloon." But I don't. It's just all mixed up in this big soup of always being moving, always being distracted, and never really knowing when one thing started and another thing ended. So, as for the focusing part before I was seven... I'm really sorry, doc, but I just don't have a clear answer for you on that one either.
Did your symptoms of restlessness and difficulty focusing continue into your teenage years?

Oh, my teenage years. Yeah. Well, see, that's where things get a lot clearer in my head, because, well, that's when everything really started to fall apart for me, to be perfectly honest. I mean, you'd think by the time a guy hits thirteen or fourteen, he'd start to mellow out a bit, right? Maybe learn how to sit in a chair without vibrating out of it. But nope. Not me. If anything, it felt like it got worse, or maybe it just mattered more, you know? 

I remember being in junior high—well, the little bit of junior high I actually managed to get through before I dropped out—and it was just torture. Absolute torture. The teachers expected you to sit there for, what, forty-five minutes at a stretch? And take notes? My leg would be bouncing so hard under the desk that the whole row of chairs would shake. I had this one teacher, Mr. Henderson, he taught history, and he would just stop dead in the middle of talking about the Civil War or whatever and just stare at me until I stopped tapping my foot. But the thing is, half the time I didn't even realize I was doing it! It was like my body had its own motor that I couldn't turn off. 

And focusing? Forget about it. I'd open a textbook, and my eyes would just slide right off the page. I'd read the same paragraph five times and have absolutely no idea what it said because my brain was off thinking about a car I saw on the way to school, or wondering how the fluorescent lights in the ceiling were wired, or just... anything else. Anything but the history book. I couldn't finish a homework assignment to save my life. I'd sit down at the kitchen table, my mom would be hovering over me, and I'd just stare at the paper until I felt like I was going to explode. I'd end up snapping my pencil or just getting up and walking out of the house because the feeling of being trapped there, trying to force my brain to do something it just flat out refused to do, was unbearable. 

So yeah, it definitely continued. It didn't magically go away when I became a teenager. It just turned into me constantly skipping class, pacing the halls, getting into arguments with teachers because I couldn't just do what they were asking me to do. It's a big part of why I never made it past the eighth grade, doc. I just couldn't handle the sitting, the listening, the trying to keep my brain on one track when it wanted to go in fifty different directions all at once. It was exhausting. Just... totally exhausting.
Did your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty focusing, cause significant problems for you during your teenage years?

Well, doc, I feel like we're kind of circling the same wagon here, because that's exactly what I was just trying to explain about junior high. The focusing part—or, you know, the total lack of it—was really the root of the biggest problems I had. I mean, I just mentioned the history book thing, right? That wasn't just a one-time deal. That was every single day, every single subject. Math, English, science, whatever they put in front of me. You ask if it caused significant problems? It basically ended my education right then and there. 

Like, I'd try, I really would. I remember sitting there with this... I think it was a science worksheet, and it had a picture of a frog on it, and I was supposed to label the parts. And I stared at that frog until my eyes literally watered, just trying to force my brain to care about what the liver or the lungs were called. But instead, I start thinking about an actual frog I caught in the creek behind our old rental house, and how it felt slimy, and then I'm thinking about the water in the creek, and then I'm wondering if the tread on my sneakers is good enough to walk on the slippery rocks... and before I know it, forty minutes have gone by, the bell rings, and my paper is completely blank. Just my name at the top, and even that was scribbled. 

So, yeah, it caused huge problems. It made the teachers think I was lazy or defiant, it made my mom cry at the kitchen table because she didn't know how to help me, and it made me feel like I was just plain dumb. Because why could everybody else in the room just look at the chalkboard, write down the assignment, and actually do it, while I felt like I was trying to climb a brick wall with no hands? It wasn't just the bouncing around and the tapping my feet, though that got me in trouble enough. It was the fact that my brain just absolutely refused to lock onto anything they wanted me to learn. So if you're asking if the inattention specifically messed things up for me back as a teenager, the answer is a hundred percent yes. Like I said, it's the whole reason I walked out of eighth grade and never went back.
Have your symptoms of restlessness and difficulty focusing been present in some form throughout your entire life?

Well, yeah, I mean, like I've been saying, the bouncing off the walls and the brain wandering off... that's always been there in the background, sure. My whole life, basically, even if the early childhood stuff is fuzzy like I told you. But... if we're talking about it being *this* bad? Like, this completely out of control and just... impossible to deal with? That's actually a different story. That's been going on for about two years and two months. 

I know that sounds super exact, two years and two months, but I know exactly when it started getting this hard to manage because that's when my older relative—he's basically been the one keeping things together for us—his health just took a massive nosedive. It was like, one day he's fine, doing his thing, and the next he's really sick, and suddenly everything just fell right on my shoulders. All the responsibilities, you know? Managing the house, trying to keep track of what needs to be done, figuring out his schedule... and for a guy who couldn't even label a frog on a worksheet in eighth grade, trying to organize a sick person's life is just an absolute nightmare. 

So, yeah, the restlessness and the focus issues, they've been my shadow forever. I've always been the guy pacing the room or zoning out. But having to actually step up and take on all these real, heavy responsibilities? It just cranked everything up to an eleven. It’s been exactly two years and two months of me just completely drowning in it. I'll try to sit down and sort out what we need to do for the week, and my leg starts going a mile a minute under the table, and my brain is just screaming at me to run out the front door. It's like the pressure of having to focus for someone else's sake just makes it all so much worse. I never really had to manage anyone else's life before, and now that I have to, it's just... it's tearing me apart, doc.
